neighbours.label: function words (' to', ' in', ' by') inside research-report framing ('the aim of this study is to', 'published in', 'we aimed to'), as against the same words in everyday prose
fire: The primary objective of this randomized trial is to compare two doses of vitamin D.
In a cohort study published in the Lancet, investigators tracked heart failure admissions.

Mortality from stroke has fallen in recent decades.
We sought to quantify the role of blood pressure control.
The purpose of the present study was to evaluate sleep quality in shift nurses.
Findings reported in the British Medical Journal suggest a link between noise and hypertension.
Investigators characterized the immune response by sequencing tumour samples from 40 patients.
This secondary analysis aimed to identify predictors of readmission after hip surgery.
Data were collected by trained interviewers using a structured questionnaire.
quiet: My grandmother takes vitamin D in the winter because her doctor told her to.
We drove to the hospital in the rain to visit my uncle after his surgery.
Last night I sat by the window and read a magazine about gardening.
The nurse brought a blanket to my room and turned off the lights.
My cousin hurt his hip in a fall and stayed in bed for a week.
I put my shoes by the door and went to sleep early.
The kids ran to the park in their new trainers after lunch.
She keeps her blood pressure cuff in a drawer by the sink.

predictions: fire 0.3-0.6 on to/in/by in research framing; everyday prose with the same words below 0.1
notes: Card: peaks on ' to' x5, ' by', '.\n' in medical abstracts ('aim of this proposed 2-year study is to', 'study published in the Journal', 'functioning of an organism by studying'). Probe: 'aim of this pilot study is to' 0.521, 'study published in the journal' 0.566, 'by studying disease' 0.384, 'We aimed to estimate' 0.453; everyday 'went to the store' 0.006, cake 0.022, chat 0.057. Near misses are everyday health sentences with the same function words.
